title: Nvidia, Microsoft and Meta Urge White House Against Restricting Open AI Models
excerpt: Three of America’s biggest tech companies warned that premature regulation of open-weight AI models would hand a competitive advantage to China.
body:
• Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta jointly warned the White House against “premature restrictions” on open-weight AI models in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick
  • The companies argued that open models drive innovation, strengthen US competitiveness, and allow global developers to build on American technology
  • The push comes as the Commerce Department weighs new export controls and access rules for advanced AI systems
  • India’s AI ecosystem, heavily reliant on open models from Meta’s Llama, could face significant disruption if restrictions proceed

Nvidia, Microsoft, and Meta issued a rare joint warning to the White House this week, urging the administration not to impose restrictions on open-weight artificial intelligence models that they say would undermine American competitiveness and hand an advantage to Chinese rivals.

The three companies sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick ahead of a key regulatory review, arguing that the openness of models like Meta’s Llama family has been a strategic asset for the United States rather than a security risk.

The Case Against Restrictions

“Premature restrictions on open-weight models would not make America safer — they would make America slower,” the letter stated. The companies argued that open models enable thousands of developers, startups, and enterprises worldwide to build on American AI infrastructure.

The intervention comes as the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security weighs new frameworks for controlling access to advanced AI systems. Proposals under consideration range from expanded export controls on model weights to licensing requirements for open-source releases above certain capability thresholds.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been particularly vocal about the risks of over-regulation. The chipmaker supplies the GPU hardware that powers virtually all frontier AI training, and any slowdown in model development directly impacts demand for its products.

The China Competition Angle

The letter specifically warned that China’s own open-model ecosystem — led by companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba’s Qwen, and Baidu — is advancing rapidly. Restricting American open models would not slow Chinese development but would push global developers to adopt Chinese alternatives.

"The Case Against Restrictions “Premature restrictions on open-weight models would not make America safer — they would make America slower,” the letter stated."

“If American open models are locked down, the rest of the world won’t stop building AI — they’ll just build it on Chinese foundations,” one industry executive involved in the lobbying effort told CNBC.

What This Means for India’s AI Sector

India’s burgeoning AI ecosystem stands to be directly affected. Indian startups and enterprises have built extensively on Meta’s Llama models for applications ranging from vernacular language processing to healthcare diagnostics. Government initiatives like India’s AI Mission have relied on the availability of open models to avoid steep licensing costs.

Indian IT services companies — including TCS, Infosys, and HCLTech — have developed custom enterprise solutions layered on open models for global clients. Restrictions that limit model access could raise costs and slow deployment timelines across the industry.

What’s Next

The Commerce Department is expected to release a proposed rule framework by the end of August, with a public comment period to follow. The outcome will have implications not just for Silicon Valley but for AI developers worldwide who have built their strategies around the assumption that open models will remain open.
